basis.text: The two commanders, in sworn testimony of 1864, put the corps' arrival at about 2 p.m. (Meade: 'did not reach the scene until about two o'clock in the afternoon'; reported to him about two; Sedgwick: 'I arrived at Gettysburg about 2 o'clock'). Meade's dispatch headed 3 p.m. has it 'just coming in' and his report says it arrived at 3; Wright has it at Gettysburg about 4 and halting two hours; Grant, Bartlett and Howe have brigades on the left about 5.

default.label: Window 14:00-17:00 on Jul 2: head 14:00-15:00 (record divided), corps about 16:00, left about 17:00
default.basis_text: Lower bound: the head about 2 p.m. in Meade's sworn testimony of 1864 and Sedgwick's, with Everett (1863) and the New Jersey narrative (1888). Inside: Meade's dispatch headed 3 p.m. (the Sixth Corps just coming in) and his report (arrived at 3), Kohler's regiment about 3, Wright about 4. Upper bound: Grant (about 5 p.m. July 2), Bartlett (a little after 5) and Howe (5) on the left center. Whether the head came in at 2 or 3 is not settled: the dispatch of the day and the later testimony may describe the head and the main body of a column 35 miles long, but no source says so.

animation.note: The head is drawn arriving at 15:00, the hour of the only dispatch of the day (the army commander's, 'just coming in'); it is not the earliest source-supported time: about 14:00 (Meade's and Sedgwick's testimony of 1864) is earlier, stays selectable and sets the floor of the arrival gate. The main body is drawn at Gettysburg about 16:00 and on the left about 17:00.

weighing.summary: The plan gives the head about 14:00 and the main body about 17:00. The record gives a spread over the afternoon. Both commanders swore in 1864 to about 2 p.m.: Sedgwick 'I arrived at Gettysburg about 2 o'clock on the afternoon of the 2d of July'; Meade, in the same inquiry, that the corps 'did not reach the scene until about two o'clock in the afternoon' and that 'it [was] reported to me about two o'clock that the 6th corps had arrived'. Everett's oration (Nov 1863) says 'not till two o'clock' and the New Jersey narrative of 1888 has the advance brigade on the field at two. Against that, Meade's dispatch to Halleck, headed 3 p.m., has the corps 'just coming in, very much worn out', and his report of 1863 says 'At 3 p. m. the Sixth Corps arrived'; a major of the Third Division puts his regiment near the field about 3; Wright and a battery commander have the corps at Gettysburg about 4 and halting about two hours; Grant, Bartlett and Howe have brigades on the left about 5. A dispatch of the day is the best class of writing, but it says 'just coming in' (the corps arriving, not its first man), and the two statements of 1864 are early narratives by the two men who were there, giving the same hour; one is the army commander who also wrote the dispatch. Both can be true of a column 35 miles long: a first report to headquarters about 2 and the corps coming in about 3, but no source says so, and the report of 1863 states 'At 3 p. m. the Sixth Corps arrived'. The best-classed evidence does not separate them, so the head is a window from 14:00 to 15:00 inside the whole window 14:00-17:00, and the 14:00 is no longer a lone memory: it is two sworn statements of 1864 by two commanders, not independent of each other as to the day (Meade says it was reported to him, perhaps by Sedgwick's staff).
weighing.who: Meade commanded the army, wrote the dispatch at his headquarters, and testified in March 1864; Sedgwick commanded the corps and testified in April 1864 about his own arrival; Wright and Howe commanded divisions; Grant, Bartlett, Kohler, Adams and Cowan commanded a brigade, a regiment and two batteries and give their own movements; Everett and the New Jersey narrative were not present.
weighing.when: Meade's dispatch is of 2 July at 3 p.m. (his own hour). Kohler wrote 1 Aug, Grant 3 Aug, Bartlett 6 Aug, Wright and Howe 7 Aug, Sedgwick's report 8 Aug, Adams 14 Aug, Cowan 15 Aug 1863; Everett 19 Nov 1863; Meade's report 1 Oct 1863; Meade's testimony 5 Mar 1864 (247 days); Sedgwick's testimony 8 Apr 1864 (281 days); the New Jersey narrative 1888.
weighing.where: The army headquarters was at the Leister house behind the cemetery. Sedgwick reports having gone there on arrival and found Meade out at the Third Corps' position; Meade says he left about 3 or half past 3 and was told about 2 that the corps had arrived. The order of Sedgwick's own story (Meade out at the front, back a few minutes later) would fit a later hour for his reporting, but that is an inference about when he reported, not when the head arrived; Sedgwick says separately that he arrived about 2 and is not shown to be wrong. Wright's 'arrived' is at Gettysburg, where the corps halted; Grant, Bartlett and Howe date the arrival on the left, after the move up. These are different places and moments, which is why the first arrival (about 2 or 3 or 4) and the 5 p.m. do not contradict each other.
weighing.how_knew: Meade wrote the dispatch the same hour and later relays a report made to him about 2; Sedgwick's hour is his own recollection of his arrival; Wright, Grant, Bartlett, Howe, Kohler, Adams and Cowan state their own units' movements; Everett and the New Jersey narrative name no source.
weighing.clock: All the witnesses are Union and no correction is applied (the plan's note of about 20 minutes between the armies' clocks plays no part here). 'About 2', 'about 3', 'about 4' and 'about 5' are read as plus or minus a quarter hour; Meade's '3 p. m.' is the hour of his dispatch.
weighing.independence: Meade's dispatch and report are one line. Meade's testimony and Sedgwick's testimony are two lines for about 2 p.m. (Meade relays a report that may have come from Sedgwick's staff); Everett (1863) is a third, not shown to be drawn from Meade, and the New Jersey narrative (1888) a fourth with no source. Wright and Adams (the artillery) are two reports for the 4 p.m.; Grant, Bartlett and Howe are three brigade and division commanders for the 5 p.m. and are independent of each other as reports, but the three brigades marched in one column. Kohler is a separate regiment.

source_panel_text: The Sixth Corps came in on Jul 2 after a march of about 35 miles. Meade and Sedgwick both swore in 1864 to about 2 p.m.; Meade's dispatch headed 3 p.m. has it 'just coming in'; Wright has it at Gettysburg about 4 and brigades reached the left about 5. The head's hour is a divided record: window 14:00-17:00. Eight other values are listed.
